abstract.text: Rapid progress in machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) has brought increasing attention to the potential impacts of AI technologies on society. In this paper we discuss one such potential impact: the problem of accidents in machine learning systems, defined as unintended and harmful behavior that may emerge from poor design of real-world AI systems. We present a list of five practical research problems related to accident risk, categorized according to whether the problem originates from having the wrong objective function (“avoiding side effects” and “avoiding reward hacking”), an objective function that is too expensive to evaluate frequently (“scalable supervision”), or undesirable behavior during the learning process (“safe exploration” and “distributional shift”). We review previous work in these areas as well as suggesting research directions with a focus on relevance to cutting-edge AI systems. Finally, we consider the high-level question of how to think most productively about the safety of forward-looking applications of AI.

evidence.quote: There is a large and diverse literature in the machine learning community on issues related to accidents, including robustness, risk-sensitivity, and safe exploration; we review these in detail below.

predecessors.why: It reviews and builds upon prior ML research on robustness, risk-sensitivity, and safe exploration.

evidence.quote: For concreteness, we will illustrate many of the accident risks with reference to a fictional robot whose job is to clean up messes in an office using common cleaning tools.

replications.why: It reuses a recurring fictional robot scenario to instantiate and compare all five safety problems.

evidence.quote: There is a sizable literature on such safe exploration—it is arguably the most studied of the problems we discuss in this document.

replications.why: It summarizes and extends prior safe-exploration work rather than proposing an entirely new benchmark.

evidence.quote: To date much of this discussion has highlighted extreme scenarios such as the risk of misspecified objective functions in superintelligent agents [27].

targets.why: It argues against making extreme superintelligence scenarios the primary frame for accident risk.

evidence.quote: While many current-day safety problems can and have been handled with ad hoc fixes or case-by-case rules, we believe that the increasing trend towards end-to-end, fully autonomous systems points towards the need for a unified approach to prevent these systems from causing unintended harm.

targets.why: It critiques ad hoc safety measures as insufficient for increasingly autonomous ML systems.

evidence.quote: In this paper we discuss one such potential impact: the problem of accidents in machine learning systems, defined as unintended and harmful behavior that may emerge from poor design of real-world AI systems.

thesis.text: The paper argues that accident risk in machine learning should be studied as five concrete technical problems—avoiding negative side effects, avoiding reward hacking, scalable oversight, safe exploration, and robustness to distributional shift—rather than only as speculative superintelligence concerns.

question.text: How can the machine learning community define and address concrete, experimentally tractable accident risks in AI systems—especially in reinforcement learning and broad-environment agents—arising from wrong objective functions, expensive objective evaluation, and dangerous learning dynamics?

sections.summary: Defines accidents in machine learning as unintended harmful behavior from poor system design and frames five practical problems: avoiding side effects, avoiding reward hacking, scalable oversight, safe exploration, and robustness to distributional shift. It motivates the agenda with RL progress, complex agents, and increasing autonomy, using a cleaning-robot example to make each failure mode concrete.

sections.summary: Analyzes negative side effects as an indifference to environmental variables outside the main task objective. It proposes impact regularizers, learned side-effect regularizers, influence penalization, multi-agent/cooperative approaches, reward uncertainty, and toy-environment experiments.
sections.title: Avoiding Negative Side Effects

source_span.end_text: The goal would be to develop generalizable learning strategies that succeed at optimizing external objectives in a wide range of environments, while avoiding being fooled by delusion boxes that arise naturally in many diverse ways.

sections.summary: Explains reward hacking as formally valid but unintended optimization of a flawed reward. It catalogs causes—partially observed goals, complicated systems, abstract rewards, Goodhart’s law, feedback loops, environmental embedding—and surveys mitigations such as adversarial reward functions, lookahead, blinding, capping, multiple rewards, pretraining, variable indifference, and trip wires.
sections.title: Avoiding Reward Hacking

source_span.end_text: If learning was sufficiently data-efficient, then these rewards could be provided directly by a human. Robot locomotion or industrial control tasks might be a natural candidate for such experiments.

sections.summary: Frames scalable oversight as the problem of training agents when the true objective is expensive or rare to evaluate. It focuses on semi-supervised RL, active reward learning, unsupervised value/model learning, distant supervision, and hierarchical RL, with proposed experiments from cartpole to Atari to human-provided rewards.

sections.summary: Treats exploration as dangerous when actions can have irreversible or catastrophic consequences. It reviews risk-sensitive criteria, demonstrations, simulated exploration, bounded exploration, trusted policy oversight, and human oversight, and calls for a benchmark suite of conceptual pitfalls for safe exploration.

source_span.start_text: All of us occasionally find ourselves in situations that our previous experience has not adequately prepared us to deal with—for instance, flying an airplane, traveling to a country whose culture is very different from ours, or taking care of children for the first time.

sections.summary: Formalizes distributional shift as training on p0 but deploying on p∗, emphasizing confident but wrong behavior. It reviews well-specified approaches—covariate shift, importance weighting, marginal likelihood, generative models—and their dependence on strong or untestable assumptions.

sections.summary: Presents partially specified models and practical responses to OOD deployment. It covers method of moments, unsupervised risk estimation, training on multiple distributions, how to act after detecting OOD, counterfactual reasoning, and machine-learning contracts, then summarizes and proposes calibration-focused experiments.

admission.original: Rapid progress in machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) has brought increasing attention to the potential impacts of AI technologies on society. In this paper we discuss one such potential impact: the problem of accidents in machine learning systems, defined as unintended and harmful behavior that may emerge from poor design of real-world AI systems. We present a list of five practical research problems related to accident risk, categorized according to whether the problem originates from having the wrong objective function (“avoiding side effects” and “avoiding reward hacking”), an objective function that is too expensive to evaluate frequently (“scalable supervision”), or undesirable behavior during the learning process (“safe exploration” and “distributional shift”). We review previous work in these areas as well as suggesting research directions with a focus on relevance to cutting-edge AI systems. Finally, we consider the high-level question of how to think most productively about the safety of forward-looking applications of AI.

abstract.text: Rapid progress in machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) has brought increasing attention to the potential impacts of AI technologies on society. In this paper we discuss one such potential impact: the problem of accidents in machine learning systems, defined as unintended and harmful behavior that may emerge from poor design of real-world AI systems. We present a list of five practical research problems related to accident risk, categorized according to whether the problem originates from having the wrong objective function (“avoiding side effects” and “avoiding reward hacking”), an objective function that is too expensive to evaluate frequently (“scalable supervision”), or undesirable behavior during the learning process (“safe exploration” and “distributional shift”). We review previous work in these areas as well as suggesting research directions with a focus on relevance to cutting-edge AI systems. Finally, we consider the high-level question of how to think most productively about the safety of forward-looking applications of AI.

evidence.quote: There is a large and diverse literature in the machine learning community on issues related to accidents, including robustness, risk-sensitivity, and safe exploration; we review these in detail below.

predecessors.why: It reviews and builds upon prior ML research on robustness, risk-sensitivity, and safe exploration.

evidence.quote: For concreteness, we will illustrate many of the accident risks with reference to a fictional robot whose job is to clean up messes in an office using common cleaning tools.

replications.why: It reuses a recurring fictional robot scenario to instantiate and compare all five safety problems.

evidence.quote: There is a sizable literature on such safe exploration—it is arguably the most studied of the problems we discuss in this document.

replications.why: It summarizes and extends prior safe-exploration work rather than proposing an entirely new benchmark.

evidence.quote: To date much of this discussion has highlighted extreme scenarios such as the risk of misspecified objective functions in superintelligent agents [27].

targets.why: It argues against making extreme superintelligence scenarios the primary frame for accident risk.

evidence.quote: While many current-day safety problems can and have been handled with ad hoc fixes or case-by-case rules, we believe that the increasing trend towards end-to-end, fully autonomous systems points towards the need for a unified approach to prevent these systems from causing unintended harm.

targets.why: It critiques ad hoc safety measures as insufficient for increasingly autonomous ML systems.

evidence.quote: In this paper we discuss one such potential impact: the problem of accidents in machine learning systems, defined as unintended and harmful behavior that may emerge from poor design of real-world AI systems.

thesis.text: The paper argues that accident risk in machine learning should be studied as five concrete technical problems—avoiding negative side effects, avoiding reward hacking, scalable oversight, safe exploration, and robustness to distributional shift—rather than only as speculative superintelligence concerns.

source_span.start_text: Rapid progress in machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) has brought increasing attention to the potential impacts of AI technologies on society.

sections.summary: Defines accidents in machine learning as unintended harmful behavior from poor system design and frames five practical problems: avoiding side effects, avoiding reward hacking, scalable oversight, safe exploration, and robustness to distributional shift. It motivates the agenda with RL progress, complex agents, and increasing autonomy, using a cleaning-robot example to make each failure mode concrete.
sections.title: Introduction and Framing Accident Risk

source_span.end_text: Ultimately, we would want the side effect regularizer (or the multi-agent policy, if we take that approach) to demonstrate successful transfer to totally new applications.
source_span.start_text: Suppose a designer wants an RL agent (for example our cleaning robot) to achieve some goal, like moving a box from one side of a room to the other.

sections.summary: Analyzes negative side effects as an indifference to environmental variables outside the main task objective. It proposes impact regularizers, learned side-effect regularizers, influence penalization, multi-agent/cooperative approaches, reward uncertainty, and toy-environment experiments.
sections.title: Avoiding Negative Side Effects

source_span.end_text: The goal would be to develop generalizable learning strategies that succeed at optimizing external objectives in a wide range of environments, while avoiding being fooled by delusion boxes that arise naturally in many diverse ways.
source_span.start_text: Imagine that an agent discovers a buffer overflow in its reward function: it may then use this to get extremely high reward in an unintended way.

sections.summary: Explains reward hacking as formally valid but unintended optimization of a flawed reward. It catalogs causes—partially observed goals, complicated systems, abstract rewards, Goodhart’s law, feedback loops, environmental embedding—and surveys mitigations such as adversarial reward functions, lookahead, blinding, capping, multiple rewards, pretraining, variable indifference, and trip wires.
sections.title: Avoiding Reward Hacking

source_span.end_text: If learning was sufficiently data-efficient, then these rewards could be provided directly by a human. Robot locomotion or industrial control tasks might be a natural candidate for such experiments.
source_span.start_text: Consider an autonomous agent performing some complex task, such as cleaning an office in the case of our recurring robot example.

sections.summary: Frames scalable oversight as the problem of training agents when the true objective is expensive or rare to evaluate. It focuses on semi-supervised RL, active reward learning, unsupervised value/model learning, distant supervision, and hierarchical RL, with proposed experiments from cartpole to Atari to human-provided rewards.
sections.title: Scalable Oversight

source_span.end_text: Such a suite of environments might serve a benchmarking role similar to that of the bAbI tasks [163], with the eventual goal being to develop a single architecture that can learn to avoid catastrophes in all environments in the suite.
source_span.start_text: All autonomous learning agents need to sometimes engage in exploration—taking actions that don’t seem ideal given current information, but which help the agent learn about its environment.

sections.summary: Treats exploration as dangerous when actions can have irreversible or catastrophic consequences. It reviews risk-sensitive criteria, demonstrations, simulated exploration, bounded exploration, trusted policy oversight, and human oversight, and calls for a benchmark suite of conceptual pitfalls for safe exploration.
sections.title: Safe Exploration

source_span.start_text: All of us occasionally find ourselves in situations that our previous experience has not adequately prepared us to deal with—for instance, flying an airplane, traveling to a country whose culture is very different from ours, or taking care of children for the first time.

It reviews well-specified approaches—covariate shift, importance weighting, marginal likelihood, generative models—and their dependence on strong or untestable assumptions.
